title: Accidental Gunshot Injury From Own Gun Qualifies For War Injury Pension: Supreme Court
case_name: JC-377745M Ex Sub Maj & Hony Lt Devi Singh v. Union of India & Ors
ratio: An injury cannot be classified as self-inflicted merely because the bullet was discharged from the serviceman's own weapon.
summary: The Court clarified that an injury cannot be classified as self-inflicted merely because the bullet was discharged from the serviceman's own weapon. The exclusion of self-inflicted injuries does not cover every accidental injury involving one's own weapon.

note.Facts: The Court clarified that an injury cannot be classified as self-inflicted merely because the bullet was discharged from the serviceman's own weapon. The exclusion of self-inflicted injuries does not cover every accidental injury involving one's own weapon.
note.Held: An injury cannot be classified as self-inflicted merely because the bullet was discharged from the serviceman's own weapon.
note.Principle: An injury cannot be classified as self-inflicted merely because the bullet was discharged from the serviceman's own weapon.

title: Magistrate Must Give Reasons When Ordering FIR Despite Police Report Of 'No Offence': Supreme Court
ratio: A Magistrate who rejects a police report stating that no cognizable offence is made out must record reasons for doing so before directing registration of…
summary: The Supreme Court has recently held that a Magistrate who rejects a police report stating that no cognizable offence is made out must record reasons for doing so before directing registration of an FIR under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC, now Section 175(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.

note.Facts: A group of landowners complained to the Delhi Economic Offences Wing (EOW) that a developer and its lenders had cheated them. The EOW, after a preliminary enquiry, filed an Action Taken Report (ATR) stating that no cognizable offence was made out. The complainants approached a Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC, and despite the ATR, the Magistrate ordered registration of an FIR. The High Court refused to quash the FIR; the appellants then appealed to the Supreme Court.
note.Issue: Whether a Magistrate must give reasons when he rejects a police report/ATR stating that no cognizable offence is made out and directs registration of an FIR under Section 156(3) CrPC (now Section 175(3) BNSS).
note.Held: The Supreme Court held that a Magistrate who rejects the police’s conclusion must record reasons relating to the material before ordering an FIR. Failure to do so renders the order “without application of mind” and is liable to be set aside.
note.Principle: A judicial authority exercising discretion under Section 156(3) CrPC must apply its judicial mind and give a reasoned order when its conclusion diverges from the investigative agency’s report; the reasons need not be elaborate but must exist and be linked to the material.
note.Provisions: - Section 156(3) CrPC (now Section 175(3) BNSS) – power to order investigation. - Action Taken Report (ATR) – not a Section 173 CrPC report (now Section 193 BNSS) and not binding, but must be considered. - References: *Lalita Kumari v. Government of UP*, *Maksud Saiyed v. State of Gujarat*, *Priyanka Srivastava v. State of UP*, *Anurag Bhatnagar v. State (NCT of Delhi)*, *SN Vijayalakshmi v. State of Karnataka*.
note.Exam angle: Test on the CrPC (or BNSS) – Section 156(3) discretion and the duty to give reasons; could be asked as “What is the requirement of reasoned orders when a Magistrate orders FIR under Section 156(3) despite police’s ATR?” – focus on judicial mind, ATR vs. Section 173 report, and relevant case law.

title: 2019 Amendment Enhancing Minimum Punishment Under POCSO Act Not Retrospective: Tripura High Court
summary: The Tripura High Court has reduced the sentence of a man convicted under the POCSO Act from 20 years to 10 years after finding that the Trial Court had applied the enhanced minimum punishment introduced by the 2019 amendment to an offence committed before the amendment came into force. Section 6 of the POCSO Act prescribes the punishment for aggravated penetrative sexual assault.

note.Facts: A man was convicted for aggravated penetrative sexual assault committed before the 2019 amendment and was sentenced to 20 years by the Trial Court.
note.Issue: Whether the enhanced minimum punishment introduced by the 2019 amendment to the POCSO Act can be applied retrospectively to offences committed before its commencement.
note.Held: The Tripura High Court reduced the sentence to 10 years, holding that the amendment is not retrospective and cannot be applied to the earlier offence.
note.Principle: An amendment increasing the minimum punishment under the POCSO Act is prospective and cannot be imposed on offences that occurred before the amendment’s commencement.
note.Provisions: Section 6 of the POCSO Act (as amended); 2019 amendment to the POCSO Act; no other cases cited.
note.Exam angle: POCSO Act – issue of retrospective application of statutory amendments; could be asked on the principle that enhanced punishments are not retrospective and the ingredients of Section 6.

case_name: M/s Kalindi Associates v. M/s Bharat Commerce and Industries Limited & Ors
summary: The Supreme Court held that a person who did not participate in an auction and is a stranger to it acquires no locus or right to seek confirmation of the bid in his favour merely by offering a higher price at a later stage.

title: 'Stringent Bail Conditions Under PMLA Cannot Override Constitutional Right To Personal Liberty': Jharkhand High Court
case_name: Basudeb Bagchi and Anr. v. Directorate of Enforcement
ratio: The stringent bail conditions prescribed under Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)…
summary: The Court observed that prolonged pre-trial incarceration, particularly where the trial is unlikely to conclude within a reasonable period, constitutes a substantial ground for granting bail notwithstanding the restrictions under the PMLA.

note.Facts: The Jharkhand High Court granted bail to two accused in a money-laundering case (Prayag Group) after they had been in pre-trial custody for a prolonged period, noting that no chargesheet was filed in the predicate offences and that the Supreme Court had already granted them bail in a related PMLA case.
note.Issue: Whether the stringent bail conditions under Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 can override the constitutional right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.
note.Held: The Court allowed bail, holding that Section 45’s restrictions cannot eclipse Article 21 and that prolonged pre-trial detention without a reasonable prospect of trial is a substantial ground for bail.
note.Principle: When pre-trial incarceration is likely to be indefinite or unduly prolonged, the statutory rigour of Section 45 PMLA yields to the constitutional guarantee of personal liberty under Article 21; bail must be granted to prevent punishment before conviction.
note.Provisions: Section 45, PMLA; Sections 3, 70, 4, PMLA; Article 21, Constitution of India; Supreme Court decisions (unnamed) on bail under Section 45.
note.Exam angle: PMLA – bail under Section 45 vis-à-vis Article 21; could be asked to frame the issue of “whether stringent statutory bail conditions can be relaxed on the ground of violation of personal liberty and right to speedy trial” and to list the ingredients (pre-trial detention length, absence of chargesheet, likelihood of early trial).

title: Jharkhand High Court Directs Improvements To AIIMS Deoghar Infra In MP Nishikant Dubey's PIL, Cites Right To Healthcare
case_name: Nishikant Dubey v. Union of India and Ors
ratio: The effective functioning of tertiary healthcare institutions such as AIIMS Deoghar is intrinsically linked to the State's constitutional obligation under Article 21 of the Constitution
summary: The Jharkhand HC has held that the effective functioning of tertiary healthcare institutions such as AIIMS Deoghar is intrinsically linked to the State's constitutional obligation under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Court observed that access to hospital facilities and timely medical care forms an integral part of the right to life and that ensuring adequate infrastructure at such institutions is not merely an administrative matter.

note.Facts: A PIL filed by MP Nishikant Dubey sought directions to make AIIMS Deoghar fully functional, highlighting deficiencies in electricity, water, fire safety, land encroachments, a railway over-bridge and a diesel-storage tank.
note.Issue: Whether the State’s failure to provide adequate infrastructure to AIIMS Deoghar violates its constitutional obligation under Article 21 to ensure the right to life-including access to timely medical care.
note.Held: The Jharkhand High Court directed the State to remedy the identified infrastructure gaps within stipulated time-frames and disposed of the PIL, noting that the State had begun remedial steps.
note.Principle: Effective functioning of tertiary-care institutions is integral to the fulfillment of the State’s constitutional duty under Article 21; therefore, ensuring essential infrastructure (electricity, water, fire safety, etc.) is a justiciable aspect of the right to life.
note.Provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution; no specific statutory sections or case citations were mentioned in the source.
note.Exam angle: Article 21 (right to life) – could be asked on how the right to health care is interpreted as part of life, focusing on the State’s duty to provide functional medical infrastructure.

title: Family Courts And High Courts Can't Grant Divorce Solely On Ground Of Irretrievable Breakdown Of Marriage: Telangana High Court
ratio: A High Court or Family Court cannot grant a decree of divorce solely on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage…
summary: The ruling: A High Court or Family Court cannot grant a decree of divorce solely on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage….

note.Facts: The Telangana High Court considered whether a decree of divorce could be granted solely on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
note.Issue: Can a High Court or Family Court grant divorce on the sole ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?
note.Held: The Court held that divorce cannot be granted solely on that ground, though it may be taken into account along with other factors when deciding a divorce appeal.
note.Principle: A decree of divorce must rest on statutory grounds; irretrievable breakdown alone is not a sufficient ground under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
note.Provisions: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (no specific section cited); not stated.
note.Exam angle: Test on the Hindu Marriage Act – ask whether irretrievable breakdown is a standalone ground for divorce and the requirement to consider additional statutory grounds.

title: 'Mere Position As School Principal Does Not Attract Liability U/S 19 POCSO Act Without Knowledge Of Offence': Patna High Court
case_name: Amal Raj v. State of Bihar and Anr
summary: The Patna HC has held that merely holding the position of Principal of a school does not automatically attract criminal liability under Sections 19 and 21 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act), unless there is material establishing knowledge or apprehension of the commission of a sexual offence and a consequent failure to discharge the statutory duty to report it.

note.Facts: The FIR alleged sexual harassment of a minor by two sports teachers; the school principal was later added as accused without any allegation of his knowledge or involvement.
note.Issue: Whether a school principal can be held liable under Sections 19 and 21 of the POCSO Act (and related provisions) merely by virtue of his position, absent proof of knowledge or apprehension of the offence.
note.Held: The Patna High Court quashed the cognizance order and all criminal proceedings against the principal, holding that his mere position does not attract liability under Sections 19, 21, 17 of the POCSO Act or Section 75 of the JJ Act without material showing knowledge, apprehension, abetment or culpable omission.
note.Principle: Liability under Section 19 POCSO (and the attendant punishment under Section 21) arises only when the person had actual knowledge or a reasonable apprehension of the offence and willfully failed to report it; mere positional authority without such knowledge is insufficient for criminal prosecution.
note.Provisions: Sections 19, 21, 17 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012; Section 75 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015; Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; reference to the Patna High Court judgment (Justice Sunil Dutta Mishra).
note.Exam angle: POCSO Act – focus on the statutory duty to report (Sec. 19) and its conditions; could be asked as an issue-framing question on “when does a person in a position of authority attract criminal liability under Sec. 19/21 POCSO?” or as an ingredient-based question testing knowledge/apprehension requirement.

title: Refunding Money To Customers Does Not Wipe Out Banking Misconduct: Calcutta High Court Upholds SBI Employee's Removal
ratio: A bank employee was required to follow prescribed procedures while handling customers' accounts, irrespective of whether the Bank ultimately suffered monetary loss
summary: The Calcutta High Court has refused to interfere with the dismissal of a former State Bank of India (SBI) employee who was found guilty of five out of six charges relating to alleged irregularities.

note.Facts: A former SBI Customer Assistant was dismissed after a departmental enquiry proved five of six charges of irregular handling of customers’ accounts, including unauthorized debits and disbursements, despite later refunds of the amounts.
note.Issue: Whether the refund of monies or the absence of financial loss can negate the misconduct and render the removal from service disproportionate.
note.Held: The Calcutta High Court dismissed the writ petition and upheld the removal, holding that refund or regularisation does not erase the misconduct already committed.
note.Principle: Refund of money or lack of loss does not extinguish the liability for misconduct; a bank employee must follow prescribed procedures, and repeated unauthorized actions constitute major misconduct justifying removal.
note.Exam angle: Could be asked under the Banking Regulation Act/Banking Service Rules – focusing on disciplinary procedure, the test of misconduct versus loss, and the proportionality of penalty.

title: Negative Phenolphthalein Test does not help accused when bribe money is placed at his direction: Kerala HC
summary: Kerala High Court : The present appeal was filed against the judgment of the Enquiry Commissioner and Special Judge, Kottayam, convicting the appellant, a former Assistant Engineer of Arakulam Gram Panchayat, for offences relating to demand and acceptance of illegal gratification under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption.

note.Facts: The appellant, a former Assistant Engineer of Arakulam Gram Panchayat, was accused of demanding and accepting illegal gratification for passing a bill on a pond construction; the complainant placed the bribe money in the measurement book (M-book) at the appellant’s direction, after which a vigilance team recovered it.
note.Issue: Whether the absence of a colour change on the appellant’s hands in a phenolphthalein test defeats the prosecution’s case of demand and acceptance of illegal gratification.
note.Held: The Kerala High Court held that the negative phenolphthalein test does not discredit the prosecution’s case, as the money was placed in the M-book on the appellant’s direction and he was apprehended before any further handling.
note.Principle: A negative phenolphthalein test on the accused’s hands does not defeat proof of demand and acceptance of illegal gratification when the money is shown to have been placed at the accused’s direction; demand and acceptance can be established by oral, documentary or circumstantial evidence.
note.Provisions: Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988; Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; cited cases: judgment of the Enquiry Commissioner and Special Judge, Kottayam; High Court judgment of A. Badharudeen, J.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the Prevention of Corruption Act – how demand and acceptance of illegal gratification are proved; focus on evidentiary issues such as the relevance of chemical tests (phenolphthalein) and the weight of oral/circumstantial evidence.
